#3730. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake’s Castle Town Has A Scene That Will Haunt Me Forever

Nintendo Switch 2The Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

I’ve been seeing some chatter online about a specific scene in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time that’s extremely beloved by longtime fans. It’s easy to miss: if you visit the Hyrule Castle Town back alleys after Zelda and Impa flee from Ganondorf, but before the time skip, you can find a soldier on the ground slumped against the wall. In the original, if you speak to him, he asks if you’re the “boy from the forest” and, in a pained stutter, tells you that Ganondorf has betrayed the king and that Zelda has escaped, but that she wanted to give something to you before she left.

His final words direct you to the Temple of Time, the text speed slowing as he finishes his line, before he shudders and fully collapses. Trying to speak to him further prompts Navi to say, “He’s not moving anymore….”, and that’s it. The soldier’s dead.

This moment has been cited by many as a prime example (among very many!) of the “darkness” of the original Ocarina of Time. It’s an otherwise noble and normal NPC dying a painful death in a back alley due to the cruelty of the villain, in front of the child protagonist who, up to this point, has only seriously fought soulless monsters. He’s not yet had to face down death in this particularly tragic way.

In the remake, however, the soldier doesn’t die. He stays alive, and you can talk to him as many times as you like to have him direct you to the Temple of Time. I believe this is just one of a cavalcade of examples of Nintendo being terrified that the player is going to get lost in the remake somehow and not know where to go. What if you forget you’re supposed to go to the Temple? He’s there to remind you, again and again, seemingly merely exhausted instead of in agony.

About the soldier in the back alley byu/dampflokfreund inOcarinaOfTime

People are bringing this up as evidence that the remake has somehow blunted the “darkness” of the original Ocarina of Time. Defanged it a bit, suggesting a more modern fear from Nintendo of exposing children to grim themes. I saw people say Nintendo “censored” itself here, or that this may have been related to “ratings.” Setting aside questions over whether or not some vague content meter of “darkness” or “maturity” is the measure of anything really, I want to push back on the idea that this moment in Castle Town has been stripped of its power: the soldier lives, yes. But for me, the remake transforms visiting Castle Town between Zelda’s departure and Link’s first experience of time travel in a way that makes it one of the most haunting and sad moments in the entire game…especially if you know what’s coming.

When you emerge in Castle Town as Adult Link in either game, it’s in ruins. Dark clouds hover over the square, and Hyrule Castle looms ominously, now the seat of Ganondorf’s power. The once-bustling square is now home to multiple horrifying Redead enemies, heavily implying that some the townsfolk may have been transformed into these health-sucking zombies. You can find most of the major NPCs from Castle Town now living in Kakariko Village, but not all of them make it there. The implication is that Ganondorf essentially enacted a massacre on the town before installing himself as king, and only a handful of refugees escaped to tell the tale.

The original Ocarina of Time had some conversationalists in Castle Town right before the timeskip, but many of the NPCs had only a little or even no dialogue, and just served as background to suggest a bustling town square. A few of those characters express some anxiety about the guy on the horse who just galloped through, if you talk to them in the brief window between Zelda’s escape and Link’s transformation. It’s the only time you can hear this special dialogue, but most of it is pretty humdrumâjust folks remarking on the horses that galloped through.

The remake’s Castle Town is populated with essentially all of the same NPCs that existed in the original, but with one key difference: just about all of them will speak to you, and most will do so at length, talking about whatever it is that’s on their mind. In that same short window of town panic right after Zelda has fled, almost everyone’s dialogue changes to remark on what just happened…but with a far deeper awareness of what’s coming than was expressed in the original game. A little girl talks about being told to stay away from the “old man chasing people.” The owner of the dog Richard spends all day and night frantically searching for him. Another wealthy woman demands answers from the guards. Some people, happy that fewer people are outside, go on a shopping spree, while one guy ponders stocking up on supplies in case of disaster. Honey and Darling continue to dance blissfully, deliberately ignoring the sound of horses.

Multiple NPCs discuss leaving town, aware that an occupation of some sort is imminent. One woman in particular suggests she might move to Goron City, but gives up the idea when she remembers she can’t eat rocks, while another puts her foot down: “Cowardsâall of you! I’m not leaving this town no matter what! I love this place.” When asked what she’ll do if the town is overrun by monsters, she stammers that she’ll “figure it out.” Maybe she’ll make friends with the monsters.

Is it weird to say I had to set the controller down for a moment after hearing all this? This whole scene was…a lot. So much more so than it was in the original. I am all-too-aware of many places in real life where people, for years and years, live extremely normal, cheerful lives. Then, something happens. Something off-putting, scary, ominous. Some folks insist everything will be fine. Others panic. Still others double down. And then, the worst thing imaginable, or even something unimaginable. People are made into victims or refugees by some force they had no power or time to stop. Harmony in one moment, horror in the next, and in between the two this tiny, surreal space of half-awareness of what might come, and disbelief that it ever could.

It’s easy to abstract the horror of all this in a video game when it’s zombies and cartoon villains. The soldier dying in the alley was sad and, sure, “dark,” but apart from a curiosity it never did much for me. Now, though, we have this haunting interlude between childhood and adulthood where these characters, briefly, exist in terrified uncertainty. These few minutes of wandering town and speaking with everyone hit me unexpectedly hard in a game that’s otherwise, relative to many other things I’ve played, pretty tame and even childish.

I think the small touch of adding all this dialogue to these NPCs in Castle Town in this moment, a moment most people will totally skip over, was a powerful and good artistic choice made by this new, younger development team. I don’t know about “dark,” I guess, or whether the remake is more so than the original. This scene has convinced me that such designations matter less than they ever did.

Presley Gerber tragically passed away after working toward addiction recovery in September of this year. He left behind his famous parents, Cindy Crawford and Casamigos businessman Rande Gerber, and his sister Kaia, who have all been reeling in the wake of his death. This week, the Bottoms cast member addressed that grief head on with a viral post about grief “coming in waves.”

It’s from The Year of Magical Thinking by Joan Didion, a book with a lighthearted title that betrays its heavy subject material and that I still think about to this day. It helped me get through my mother’s battle with cancer, and I think it’s a helpful read for anyone going through it with a loved one. However, it particularly highlights grief in the face of addiction, and I would guess was especially pertinent to Gerber.

Kaia shared a post this week about the titles on grief that have been helpful after losing her brother. A separate slide included a quote from Didion that's one of the more memorable from the book.

Grief, when it comes, is nothing we expect it to be. Grief has no distance. Grief, comes in waves, paroxysms, sudden apprehensions that weaken the knees and blind the eyes and obliterate the dailiness of life.

Here's what else she's been reading in recent days, per her post.

A post shared by Library Science (@libraryscience)

Didion wrote The Year of Magical Thinking in 2005, while frequenting hospitals as her daughter Quintana Roo dealt with health issues. All of this came just shortly after losing her husband, beloved author John Gregory Dunne. The book follows Didion’s experience with grief following her husband’s death alongside her daughter’s hospitalizations and complications related to alcohol abuse. The book ends without us knowing what was next for Quintana Roo and Didion, though her daughter would pass away in August of 2005, just shortly before the author would publish the book.

Joan Didion mixes up stories about experiences she'd shared with her family over time with prose about everything she was also going through in the moment. It’s beautiful, direct, and devastating writing. I wouldn’t recommend picking it up as a beach read, but if you are going through something in your family, it’s helpful for contextualizing feelings and realizing humans are similar. We all go through the pain and anger and feelings of helplessness when we are losing a loved one.

It's not one of the author's titles that have yet made it to the big screen, but Didion’s book is powerful. I read almost 10 years ago and some of her words are still with me. It holds up years after it was published, and it’s a gripping read. I’m glad Kaia Gerber found solace in it. I hope her parents, and celebrity pals like George and Amal Clooney, have found some solace too.

#3727. Stellar Blade On Switch 2 Looks Like A Great Port, Until You Start Fighting

There's no denying that Stellar Blade is one seriously good-looking game. On Switch 2, it runs surprisingly well on Nintendo's hybrid system, and it'd be a perfect port if it wasn't for one glaring issue that holds it back.

On the surface, Stellar Blade looks like a smooth port with few compromises, as it still offers plenty of graphical detail at a lower resolution. Stellar Blade on Switch 2 also targets 60fps, but in order to achieve that, it uses a very aggressive form of frame generation to create a smooth sense of action. The problem with this is that it makes the game harder to play, because your actions are delayed.

Parries and dodges require perfect timing, and because the game is delayed, pressing a button right as an enemy hits you is often too late, causing you to take damage. This also means that controlling the protagonist Eve feels somewhat sluggish, navigating the environments feels sluggish, and during chaotic fights, the game can lag so badly that it feels like your controller is completely ignoring your inputs. This is at odds with how the game teaches you to master its gameplay, as the natural rhythm you're supposed to pick up alongside visual cues simply does not match up with the delicate timing needed to pull off counters and parries.

Because Stellar Blade is an action game that's tightly centered on strict frame windows for counters and dodges--think of it as being soulslike-adjacent with its combat--the disconnect between the 60fps visuals and the heavier 30fps input feel makes precise timing noticeably harder to hit.

Developer Shift Up was aware of this, as after it received player feedback from the Stellar Blade Switch 2 demo, it added a Frame Generation Toggle to the game's settings. Turning it off will make the game run at a visually native frame rate, and it removes the extra buffer, which goes a long way toward making controller responsiveness feel tighter. Your mileage may vary, and if you can overcome the unnatural timing behind defensive moves in Stellar Blade on Switch 2, there's plenty to love about it.

But if you have a decent PC or a PS5? Stellar Blade plays much better on those platforms, even if you can't take them on the go with you. The Switch 2 edition does include some nice extras like Bayonetta outfits and all of the post-launch content, so if you're eyeing a purchase of Stellar Blade on it, grab the demo and see if you can get to grips with how the game plays on that platform.

Shift Up is also working on a sequel, Stellar Blade: Blood Rain, which features a new pint-sized powerhouse of a protagonist.

#3726. Bonfire of the Neocons: The MAGA Finger-Pointing Begins

Good afternoon from Washington, where foie gras is now illegal and the local Stasi is going door-to-door to check that every citizen has downloaded Bluesky.

The town, one of the bluest in the country, is in a state of stunned ecstasy as it struggles to process the mind-bending midterm election results. Democrats won the House, the Senate, and a majority of governorships, penetrating deep into historically red strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina. During a book party for Sophia Bush at The Jefferson hotel on Wednesday night, the actor nearly cried as she delivered a toast to the results—and to her new bestseller.

On the right, the finger-pointing has already begun. In this edition of Party Animals, you can read my dispatch from a night out with the DC Republicans in mourning and the Democrats celebrating in cocktail-fueled delirium. Plus, a MAGA civil war reignites over Iran, with Vice President JD Vance already wading into the factional fight that could determine the future of the party.

Also mentioned in this issue: Marc Thiessen, Curt Mills, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott, James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Mark Mitchell, Matt Walsh, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be drowned in cocktail-fueled delirium. Praise will be run as a Democrat south of the Mason-Dixon Line.

The morning after the generational Republican midterm collapse that Party Animals is dubbing Blue Tuesday, JD Vance put on his political-analyst cap. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy X post. “The president himself said so last night.”

Never mind that Vance’s referenced war is one that his own administration started and is currently presiding over. Vance has often tried to cast himself as an outside observer of the Trump administration, its preeminent reply guy on social media and podcasts—a clever, if often ludicrous, pose for the vice president.

The Vance post was the highest-level opening salvo in a civil war that had been brewing for some time. It erupted into the open on Tuesday night as the results began to spell doom for Republicans and the blame started flying with velocity. The internecine battle is between the “America First” faction of the Trump movement and those who have supported the war in Iran, the latter labeled by detractors—with a sneer—as neocons.

The day before the blue tsunami, hopeful MAGA devotees attended a campaign rally in Ohio.

“The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” wrote Matt Walsh in a post on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.” As the dire results came down, even some on the right who had cheered on the war came to see, in the cold glow of their screens, the political devastation it had wrought. “Iran War is clearly catastrophically unpopular and has to end,” posted Will Chamberlain, who had spent the last few months loudly dismissing the war’s critics as subliterate simpletons.

On social media, MAGA luminaries shared a screenshot of an infamous op-ed written by Iran war booster Marc Thiessen, whose headline confidently claimed earlier this year: “There is no US downside to striking the Iranian regime.” Fox host Mark Levin lashed out at critics blasting his support for the war, insisting it had nothing to do with the results. Reality would seem to differ. One NBC News exit poll found that 74% of voters said Iran was a “crucial or major factor in how they voted.”

“It was the Iran war, stupid,” said Curt Mills, the executive director of The American Conservative, in an interview with Party Animals. Speaking about Thiessen and Levin, Mills was unsparing: “Professional liars. Professional liars. Not analysts, not honest people, and, honestly, not very invested in the future of the country.”

I asked Mills, who praised Vance’s statement, if it was not strange for the vice president to speak out against the administration while serving in it. “What option does he really have if he wants to keep his job, stop the war, and maybe run for president? I mean, it is strange. It is unprecedented in some ways,” he said. “Is it working? Maybe.”

In restaurants and barrooms across the capital, the ruling party’s apparatchiks watched and agonized as Democrats mounted a historic midterms rout.

The How: The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and colleagues have the definitive account of how Trump lost the midterms for Republicans, packed with genuinely shocking reporting that reveals exactly what went wrong at each turn.

Rockstud the Vote: My colleague José Criales-Unzueta trained his gimlet eye on a photo posted by Free Press reporter Olivia Reingold from a Democratic election night party in Michigan and found some suspicious discrepancies in the leather straps of a smoking heel.

Ballroom Blues: Read Shawn McCreesh’s New York Times dispatch from Trump’s strange walk of shame around the White House ballroom construction site the morning after the midterms. “Inside his concrete chrysalis,” McCreesh writes, “everything was still beautiful.” 💔

Department of (Deeply Unpopular) War: Amid a flurry of anonymous quotes from Trump officials and allies laying blame for the midterms on Pete Hegseth, the president tells Jonathan Karl of ABC News that he’s standing by his defense secretary—for now, at least.

Of Mics and Men: In the wake of Patrick Bet-David’s election night stream, Vanity Fair’s Dan Adler has a biting eulogy for the manosphere: “Donald Trump’s 2024 tour of the Joe Rogan–dominated podcast circuit heralded the makings of a new mainstream media. But in the MAGA midterm wreckage, the idea of the manosphere as a political force has shattered.”

A Few Good Streamers: VF’s Abigail Sylvor Greenberg spoke with Hasan Piker and his lawyer, who promised that Piker’s $75 million defamation lawsuit against Scott Jennings is only the beginning.

Russell Brand trial: The star comedian turned right-wing podcast lounge lizard was found guilty in a London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Musk in the barrel: Elon Musk, who just torched nearly half a billion dollars in an effort to keep Republicans in power, now faces the wrath of Democrats. The New York Times has a handy guide to the coming storm. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Senator Ed Markey.

Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios.

When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.

The highest of the highs have been all the talented and wonderful people I’ve worked with and grown to love: the DC Studios crew, our talented collaborators, our casts and crews, and the boisterous and hilarious fans. And the best part of all has been working with Peter Safran, the smartest and most competent person I know. You’ve been the best partner a person could ask for, and, more so, a truly good friend.

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years (Jenn, I love you and I’m sorry and you don’t need to feel guilty for being the happiest of all people that I’m no longer doing this job). And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I’m incredibly passionate about and the ones I’m not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head.

So, yes, I will miss the people around me, and I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking. That’s not to say Peter and 1 are immediately done with DC or superheroes. We have Man of Tomorrow out this summer. And we’ve just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing, and we’ll see where it goes after that. And, of course, the characters we set up will live on.

Thank you so very, very much for embracing the characters and stories we’ve put on screen.

#3724. Nintendo’s Wisest Investment Continues To Pay Off With Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

We should acknowledge that Monolith Soft isn't just a Xenoblade developer, but also a major supporter of The Legend of Zelda franchise. The studio confirmed on X that it assisted with programming and graphics (per a machine translation) on the Ocarina of Time remake. This marks the fifth time the team has contributed to a mainline Zelda title, starting with 2011's Skyward Sword. 

There were a lot of theories in the past couple of months about what team was behind The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2--especially considering the visual overhaul and the Internet's reaction. Earlier this week, Nintendo revealed that its internal team responsible for Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3, was responsible for the remake. We now know that Monolith Soft also pitched in, as the team did with the two Switch mainline entries, too.

In 2007, Nintendo acquired Monolith Soft from Bandai Namco, with the developer at the time working on Disaster: Day of Crisis for Wii. The studio was probably best known for the Xenosaga series, but it's doubtful anyone could predict how prolific Monolith Soft would become over the past 19 years. 

Just looking at Monolith Soft's portfolio, the developer has already contributed to three Switch 2 heavy hitters: Ocarina of Time, Splatoon Raiders, and Mario Kart World. This is all in addition to overseeing and creating the Xenoblade franchise, with Xenoblade Genesis planned for release next year. It's an impressive resume. 

Zelda: Ocarina of Time producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi recently chatted with GameSpot about the game's development. The Switch 2 exclusive released yesterday, November 5, and is already wearing out the screenshot button for Steve Watts. You can see how gorgeous the remake is compared to the Nintendo 64 original.

#3721. “We Failed,” Take-Two Boss Says Of The Mega-Flop Borderlands Movie

2024's Borderlands movie was a massive flop at the box office, and Take-Two's CEO has now reacted to this, readily acknowledging, "We failed."

Speaking at Business Insider Live, Strauss Zelnick said Take-Two's mission is to "make the best entertainment on Earth," and with the Borderlands film, the company failed to meet that mark.

He said the company "tried incredibly hard" on the Borderlands movie, and pointed out that Take-Two didn't actually lose any money on it because Lionsgate funded it. "But I am here to tell you, it was not the best entertainment on Earth. We failed," he said.

The Borderlands movie featured a stacked cast of big names, including Cate Blanchett as Lilith, Kevin Hart as Roland, Jack Black as the voice of Claptrap, Ariana Greenblatt as Tiny Tina, and Jamie Lee Curtis as Tannis. The film was directed by Eli Roth, with Tim Miller stepping in for reshoots.

The Borderlands movie made just $15.5 million in the US and $17.5 million internationally for a total of only about $33 million worldwide.

Zelnick said this in response to a question about why Take-Two doesn't do more in terms of adapting its franchises for film, TV, theme parks, and live events. He said Take-Two is "very selective" when it comes to these kinds of projects. "If our mission is to make the best entertainment on Earth, we only want to make a movie if it's going to be the best entertainment on Earth," he said.

But with the Borderlands film, Zelnick said, "We failed across our mission."

"Culture, like character, is tested in the breach. When things are going well, it's convenient to say yes. But your test is when there is a challenge. And you either believe in your mission or you don't," he said. "So if we can be the best at something, and deliver a phenomenal experience, we still have to make money while we're at it. This is not a non-profit enterprise, and by the way, we're not curing cancer. I am charged by my shareholders to deliver a return, I just believe the best way to deliver a return is to do the best work you can."

While the Borderlands movie didn't work out, Take-Two isn't giving up with transmedia efforts, as a BioShock movie is now in the works at Netflix. The Hunger Games veteran Francis Lawrence is set to direct the movie ... if it ever happens.

Minor spoilers ahead for Episode 2 of The Gilded Age Season 4.

Shortly after its debut, Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. Fans of Downton Abbey were thrilled at the new series set in America (streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and we're two episodes into its fourth season on the air. The show is full of Broadway royalty, and two more stars of the Great White Way have just joined the fun. So what is it going to take to get a full-blown musical episode?

The Gilded Age Season 4 started off with a bang, with fans concerned about Marian and Larry's relationship after their tryst. The Gilded Age cast is obviously full of Broadway icons, such as Audra McDonald, Kelli O'Hara, Denée Benton, Donna Murphy, and Celia Keenan-Bolger. Now we've got two more with Bonnie Milligan and Taylor Trensch joining the fun in the new season.

Milligan plays Mrs. Louisa Knapp Curtis, a journalist who is covering President Cleveland's forthcoming visit to New York. She won the Tony for her role in Kimberly Akimbo, and she also originated the role of Pamela in Head Over Heels.

Theater kids like me also likely clocked that Taylor Trensch recently made his debut on The Gilded Age as well. He's playing Oliver, the new bumbling footman for the van Rhijn household. I was first introduced to his work on stage in Bare: The Musical, but he's also been seen on Broadway in Dear Evan Hansen, Wicked, Hello, Dolly! and more. It seems like Oliver is going to be struggling with the new gig, although I'm going to be waiting for him to belt out some tunes in every scene.

With so many Broadway stars part of the massive Gilded Age cast, it feels like having a musical episode is a no-brainer. We've seen various shows have these types of specials before, including Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Scrubs, and Grey's Anatomy. None of those titles had the amount of accomplished musical theater performers that the HBO series has, so I'd imagine that The Gilded Age would blow people away if it allowed its cast to show off their vocal talents.

I'm not the only one who has been hoping to see a musical episode of The Gilded Age. While it remains to be seen if this happens, fans were treated to Voices of The Gilded Age: The Christmas Album, which features the cast of the show singing holiday tunes. That's the closest thing we've got to a musical episode for the time being, but maybe it'll help drum up excitement for that to happen in the future. Fingers crossed.

The Gilded Age airs new episodes Sundays on HBO As part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll have to see if I ever get my wish of a full-blown musical episode, but for now I'll be streaming the Christmas album.

#3719. Bob Dylan Meets Pope Leo in a Black Hoodie and Polka-Dot Tie

Yes, I was there. Not at his meeting with the pope, of course, but at the controversial Bob Dylan concert held at the Unipol Dome in Milan.

The legendary singer-songwriter has a discography that stands the test of time, but his recent decision to perform in near darkness hasn’t exactly been celebrated. With a black hood pulled up that almost completely conceals his face and only a few dim lights illuminating the stage, the impact of seeing one of the greatest artists of the 20th century was greatly diminished. From the stands, I couldn’t even zoom in on my phone because it was sealed in a bag at the entrance.

Eventually, I accepted it. Dylan intentionally created this experience, expressing his desire to distance himself from the audience. Far from a technology-forward performance, the Nobel Prize laureate, whose face has become a central figure in modern history, sang nonstop from under a hood for more than an hour and a half.

Dylan has worn the hood for at least the last two years, likely because he wants the audience to focus on his music rather than on him as a public figure. But does it have the same effect when meeting with the pope, especially when he isn’t performing?

The singer was received by Pope Leo XIV at the Apostolic Palace, dressed as if it were a stop on his tour: black sweatshirt, hood up, black gloves, black pants, and a loosely tied polka-dot tie. The ensemble was completed by an umbrella—also black—being used as a cane.

Andrea Monda, editor in chief of the Vatican newspaper L’Osservatore Romano, and Reverend Antonio Spadaro, an official from the Vatican’s Ministry of Culture, which sponsored this meeting, as it had done in July with Patti Smith, escorted Dylan. The two Americans came together in a tableau that is destined to become iconic.

The contrast bordered on the surreal: The Pope's characteristic white robes and Dylan's reclusive black hood. As always, the memes were quick to follow. Some compared Dylan to Palpatine from Star Wars, while others saw a parallel to the final encounter in the game Assassin’s Creed II.

It’s amusing to see them visually contrasted, because their personalities overlap in many ways (and not just because of their American origins). Pope Leo wrote the foreword to a book on disarmament, quoting a 1963 protest song by Dylan titled “Go Away You Bomb.” As for Dylan, he has embarked on a spiritual journey over the years that has brought him closer to the Christian faith.

Pope Leo XIV meets Bob Dylan on November 4, 2026, in Vatican City, Vatican.

“I’m a religious person,” he said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal—“I read the scriptures a lot, meditate and pray, light candles in church. I believe in damnation and salvation, as well as predestination. The Five Books of Moses, Pauline Epistles, Invocation of the Saints, all of it.”

So, is wearing a hood in the presence of the Pope a provocation? Probably not: If anything, it’s consistent with how he has made his recent public appearances.

The brief, 10-minute meeting was private, during which the two exchanged gifts. The Pope gave Dylan a rosary. The musician reciprocated with a signed copy of Chronicles–Volume One, Dylan’s autobiography. The hood stayed on throughout the meeting, turning a gesture of artistic consistency into something that, to outsiders, might look like a defensive maneuver.

Perhaps this is the intended paradox: Dylan has spent his career evading labels, yet precisely when he tries to hide, his goes viral. In many ways, it’s an act of loyalty to himself. At 85, with a career that has left an indelible mark on music and politics, he continues to defy conventions. At least he took off his gloves to shake the Pope’s hand.

(Photo by Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)

#3718. Nier Automata’s File Size Now Reflects How Good It Is

Nier Automata is my favorite game of all time, and I've been telling everyone I know to play it for nearly a decade. On PC, however, Square Enix accidentally made that a little bit more difficult, because the game's latest patch ballooned the game's file size by more than 600%.

The update, tested by RPG Site, takes what was a pretty reasonable 50GB file size and raises it to 366GB. It appears to be incorrectly assigning a file size of more than 40GB to each piece of DLC. The patch itself was supposed to simply add three new languages to the Steam version: Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Korean.

"We are currently investigating the cause and working to resolve the issue. We apologize for the inconvenience," Square Enix said in a post on Steam.

Because the giant file size is linked to the different pieces of DLC, you can temporarily resolve the issue by going to "Properties" and "DLC" on Steam and unselecting them. Of course, this also means you won't be able to enjoy that DLC, so if you mostly want to fight the former CEO of Square Enix in the game, you're going to have to wait.

As for what's next for the Nier series, Square Enix and director Yoko Taro have been pretty hush-hush, but Automata has been an immense success. As of February 2026, it had sold more than 10 million units. An anime adaptation is also available now on Crunchyroll.

#3717. Has The Ocarina Of Time Remake Changed Too Much? Fans Debate Difficulty, Tone, And Handholding

As is often the case when something is remade, the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is generating a lot of comparisons to the original. Purists will often deride any changes made to the thing they grew up with, so I was prepared for a lot of the discussion to come off like an old man yelling at cloud about how one of the most widely celebrated video games of all time was better âback in his day.â However, the Ocarina of Time remake isnât just getting a lot of the usual remake criticism that tends to revolve around things like graphical fidelity and art style; thereâs also a fair bit of discussion about how its modern game design sensibilities may have sanded off some edges and, in so doing, diminished certain things that made Ocarina of Time great.

This morning, I came across a 16-minute video in which Twitter user KloverKlub14 rattled off most of their complaints about the remake. Some of them can be dismissed as nitpicking small details that only the sickest of sickos would ever recognize, but thereâs actually a fair bit here that stood out to me about how much easier Ocarina of Time is on Switch 2 than it ever was on the Nintendo 64.

I compiled most of my complaints with the Ocarina remake into this video pic.twitter.com/tnnNx9Jslc

— KloverKlub (@KloverKlub14) November 8, 2026

In the flood of complaints, a theme emerges. The difficulty nerf isnât as easy to sum up as saying âLink does more damage than before,â but instead manifests in several little things that add up across the course of the game. Certain environmental hazards are gone, Link no longer lands on a lower floor if he plummets off certain platforms but instead just respawns where he fell from, some enemy behaviors like Stalfos being able to revive themselves if you donât defeat an entire squad of them quickly enough have been removed, and some secrets in the environment are now signposted with elements like dedicated targets for Link to aim the Hookshot at, denying players the pleasure of figuring it out for themselves (or sparing them the effort, depending on how you feel about the change).

âPeople keep pointing at better controls and âit was harder for you before because you were a child,â conveniently ignoring that people continued to replay this game into their adulthood,â a redditor writes. âBut it goes beyond that, for both the puzzle and navigation aspect and combat, there are factually things that make it easier. Some dungeon challenges are simplified, objects in the room are less hidden and easier to spot, there’s constant exposition for what you’re supposed to do, challenges that used to be timed now no longer have a timer. Some enemies are easier, some are actually harder, like the Redeads now being more aggressive and able to run. Those changes can be subjective, but there are also changes that objectively make it easier, like Stalfos dealing half the damage they used to. On the other hand, I’ve noticed heart drops are more scarce, and I’ve never seen enemies drop three hearts like they frequently did in the original. Other examples are King Dodongo now being less of a joke, since you can no longer just stand to the side as he rolls past you, and he now also summons baby dodongos. But then there’s bosses like Phantom Ganon who is significantly easier with the slow moving energy balls.â

Finished Ocarina remake. Pretty conflicted overall. I think this is a death by a thousand cuts situation honestly. There are too many little things that I loved about the original game that have been lost here.

Something Iâve definitely noticed is that some parts of the Ocarina of Time remake feel like theyâre shying away from the darkness of the original game. Yes, I am comparing the level of dread and fear I felt playing the game as a kid to what I feel now as an adult, but Iâm specifically thinking of the original gameâs more explicit references to the violent deaths of people who arenât villains. One notable example that a lot of fans have pointed out is that at the end of the gameâs first act, when Zelda has fled Castle Town and Ganondorf has gone after her, thereâs a soldier who can be found in the back alleys of the town that was originally mortally wounded. The original Ocarina of Time made it pretty clear that he had died from his injuries trying to save Zelda, with the text after his dying words saying âheâs not moving anymore,â but that text no longer appears in the remake. Instead, you can talk to this man as many times as you want.

I found the solider! pic.twitter.com/Y0ZUFVlqBB

— Steve (@StupidhanyEne) November 5, 2026

Another thing Iâve seen circulating is that some believed blood stains that appeared throughout the Shadow Temple had been removed, as you no longer see the blood-red puddles underneath what look like crucifixes. However, as others have pointed out, old, dried blood wouldnât retain the same crimson color that fresh blood does, so the darker smears that appear in the remake are actually more accurate.

I suspect the young development team wanted to bring back the bloodstains in the OoT well, but were probably told no.

The result was probably this middle ground of very old stains, just not red. #Zelda pic.twitter.com/SKUsUshcMZ

— Mighty (@MightyGazelle1) November 6, 2026

âItâs funny how the more realistic implementation of this with faded dry blood is easier to sneak into an E10 game because it can be passed off as dirt or rust,â a fan writes on Reddit. âThe bright red blood of the OG isâ¦ bloodier, obviously, but arguably more cartoony.â

These are smaller details, but thereâs also a pretty major scene in the endgame that no longer includes a character coughing up blood. To avoid spoilers, weâll just link the comparison here if you want to click on it. Given how much more detailed Ocarina of Time looks on the Switch 2, itâs possible Nintendo omitted this to avoid a T for Teen rating with the ESRB. Most Zelda games are either rated E or E10+, with the exception of Twilight Princess, which got a T rating back in 2006 and is widely considered the âdarkestâ game in the series.

While changes are a big part of the conversation, another is whether or not Nintendo played it too safe when remaking Ocarina of Time. One major point of contention is that Hyrule Field, the overworld players pass through as they head from one town to the next, feels just as empty as it did on the N64, though some donât think it needed to get peppered with enemies and activities,Â

âBack in 1998, Hyrule Field was a nice little tech demo that allowed Nintendo to show off how the N64 could render some really big triangles, just to make the poor old PlayStation look bad,â Moon Game Studios CEO Thomas Mahler says on Twitter. âBut from a design perspective, it was already pretty lousy back then. And to simply copy that design 1:1 today? Nah. Every designer at Nintendo should be crying foul and know that this could be done so much better nowadays.â

not to be a hater or maybe itâs a bad cIip, but there just being Iike a giant empty fieId with Iike nothing going on feeIs so sIoppish to me.whyâs everything gotta be boring open worId slop https://t.co/RpX8VuzXdd

— toby (@The_Bees_Sneeze) November 9, 2026

âI think Hyrule Field being largely empty allows the world to breathe and gives the game a sense of scale and immersion,â New Blood Interactiveâs Mark Diaz argues. âPlayers don’t always need to be bombarded with activities, sometimes it’s nice to just exist in the game world and be alone with your thoughts. I grew up in the middle of nowhere in North Carolina. In real life, nature is like that sometimes, just a lot of trees and grass and rocks and leaves, with nothing particularly important or interesting going on, and that’s okay! Hyrule Field felt familiar to me in that way.â

Overall, the Ocarina of Time remake is an interesting case study in both how much and how little game design has changed in the years since the original. Is it a solid way to experience one of the most beloved games of all time, or does it feel like a sanitized replica of something that didnât need to be modernized in this way? Or is it just kind of a cool thing to exist that doesnât have any bearing on your feelings on the original and brings a special game to a new audience? Thatâs in the eye of the beholder, I suppose.Â

What this does make me very curious about is how Nintendo might handle a hypothetical Majoraâs Mask remake. That game has a lot more friction and challenging systems than Ocarina of Time, and I wonder if Nintendo might excise some of those for a modern audience. There are hints that such a remake might be coming in the future, but thereâs been no official announcement as of right now.

#3716. Porsha Williams Brings 'Unbothered' Energy to 'Real Housewives of Atlanta'

Porsha Williams has had quite the fill of juicy drama in Atlanta, but after a cross-country trip with some of Bravo’s most legendary Housewives, this Georgia peach is coming home with thicker skin and a much harder-to-bruise attitude.

The Real Housewives of Atlanta star, 45, exclusively told Us how filming The Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip: Roaring 20th taught her that a little shade doesn’t have to leave a bitter taste, especially when surrounded by women who know how to hold their own.

“What I took from doing the show with them is the confidence that each lady had because these are the best of the best from each city,” Williams told Us, referring to costars Gizelle Bryant, Teresa Giudice, Luann de Lesseps and Kyle Richards. “ I took their confidence and I took them being unbothered with me back to Atlanta.”

Although Williams is notorious for squashing digs with her signature line, “Who said that?”, fans watched her decades-long friendship with Shamea Morton sour during season 16 of RHOA after Morton, 44, became a full-time member of the franchise.

Ahead of season 17, Williams said she had hoped for a fresh start, previously sharing with Us in April that she wanted to put prior conflicts aside and welcome new friendships. “I just wanted a clean slate, and I wanted to have a good time. I wanted to be open to new friendships… and have this season feel like a breath of fresh air,” she said at the time.

That hope was tested when tensions continued to boil over into season 17 during a cast trip to Scotland, where the two officially declared their friendship was over after a heated dinner exchange—a rift that remained unresolved at the reunion.

Rather than promising a drama-free future, Williams said she’s trying to draw a line between playful disses and personal attacks, with a new focus on fostering sisterhood rather than fueling conflict.

“I’m also taking from Ultimate Girls Trip a lighter tone for the season,” Williams told Us.” I’m trying to set that in everything that I do. It’s not always about going below the belt and, like, ruining somebody’s life or career. So I’m bringing back fun shade.”

With hopes of taking a fuzzier approach to navigating on-screen battles in season 18, Williams says her standards were set long before she ever held a peach, and she’s equally intentional about what she hopes to pass down to her 7-year-old daughter, Pilar Jhena McKinley.

“[The] No. 1 thing for me as a mom and being a mom to a beautiful child like Pilar is to make sure that she feels good about what she does,” Williams said. “I let her speak life into herself, which helps her build her own confidence in anything that she does. So it’s not just someone telling her that she’s great, or someone telling her she’s had high standards, she knows it for herself.”

During Charmin’s Wider Sheet Immersive NYC Experience, where the reality TV star partnered with Charmin Ultra Strong to celebrate the brand’s newest innovation, she recalled how her mother, Diane Williams (Ms. Diane), instilled high expectations in her from an early age — right down to toilet paper.

“I think I was born with high standards, and then I just started raising them above and above and above,” she told Us. “I don’t think I’ve ever really had low standards.”

The mother of one also credits her younger sister, Lauren Williams, with how she raises her own daughter, revealing that watching how they encouraged their own children helped develop her understanding of self-worth.

“In my world of reality TV, often people feel like, ‘oh, it’s what you tell me I am’, no, it’s not. It’s what I say I am,” Williams told Us. “It’s how I say I feel about me, and so my life lessons, my little sister, my mom, they helped me parent very well for Pilar.”

#3715. Bill Skarsgard Didn’t Need Much Convincing To Join Hideo Kojima’s Physint

Hideo Kojima's Physint has a leading man in Bill Skarsgård, and the Hollywood actor recently spoke more about his part in the game. Billed as a spiritual successor to Kojima's Metal Gear Solid franchise, Physint is an action-espionage game that features Skarsgård alongside several other actors, like Charlee Fraser, Don Lee, and Minami Hamabe. Skarsgård's love for the Metal Gear Solid franchise and a chance to work with Kojima proved to be the deciding factors in taking on the role of the unnamed Physint protagonist.

"I played every single one," Skarsgård said to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. "Starting from the one on PlayStation One all the way to the last one. I was very enamored by him [Kojima], the mythology and the universes that he creates, but also the mystique and the allure about him, as well. He is an auteur, but he's a video game auteur. He's fluent in filmmaking, and film, and cinema."

Skarsgård believes that Kojima's cinematic video games are a new medium that he's pioneering, and with Physint, the developer is getting closer to "something that's photorealistic and also interactive," the actor said. "I think he's a pioneer, and he keeps going out to untreaded waters."

Kojima is also a fan of Skarsgård, and he recently spoke about how he was introduced to him through a mutual acquaintance, Death Stranding 2: On the Beach composer Yoann "Woodkid" Lemoine. After traveling to Sweden to meet Skarsgard and his family, Kojima pitched him the lead role in Physint, which Skarsgard accepted.

While it looks like production on Physint is starting to pick up steam, it's still early days for the project. Kojima previously revealed that the script for it is ready, but there's still work to be done on motion-capture and filming performances. Sony was originally funding development on it, but after the PlayStation company pulled support for it, Kojima found a new home at Xbox for Physint. The developer has described Physint as the "biggest-selling" game that he could possibly create, and Xbox is also funding development on his upcoming horror game, OD Knock.

I’m Fascinated By One Survivor Castaway Who Is Getting An Almost Comically Negative Edit

A Survivor 51 Castaway Is Not Pleased With Jeff Probst And Called Him Out On Social

I Think Mike Pinsky Can Still Win Survivor 51, But I’m Officially Writing Off 3 Other Castaways

I truly cannot believe I'd ever be this hungry.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Survivor's Lewis Kelly made my stomach turn with this "wtf" story about just how hungry contestants get. I'd suspected things could get dire when I've seen players give up immunity for food, but never in a million years did I think people would consider eating food they pooped out.

As we watch him try to win it all on the 2026 TV schedule, Lewis recalled a shocking story on TikTok in which someone in the tribe made a wild suggestion after Sharonda came back with corn. He explained below:

As you know corn does not fully digest when you poop. Someone in our camp noticed that we were pooping out corn kernels and thought that we could reuse them. Wanted us to pick them out of our poo, wash them, and reboil them in a pot and see if we could get a second use out of them...That merge feast came at the perfect time I have to say.

Keep in mind, Survivor contestants are getting fed more these days than they were a long time ago. I just can't imagine who was suggesting that they genuinely pick corn out of their own fecal matter, combine it, and then boil it to serve in another meal. Literally every time I type that out, I get the urge to vomit, so I'm not sure how anyone could legitimately consider it.

Survivor's Brady Got Asked About The Peeing Thing (But I Can't Get Over How Many Times He Said Brody)

Sharonda received the corn when the Dina tribe was still together, which leads me to wonder who among them suggested such a wild thing. The only thing I can think of is that Danny Kilby has gone on the record about his love of pooping in the ocean, and how it may be his preferred way of doing that. Is there any connection between these stories? We can only speculate.

It's stories like this that make me empathize more with Survivor contestants when they crash out over not being picked to eat an Applebee's reward. I would've never thought food could be such a factor, especially when the game was reduced to 26 days, but Lewis just drove home for me how desperate things can get.

The good (and perhaps most important) part of the story is that it seemed like no one was actually game to do it. Had that post-merger feast never happened, however, we might've heard about some Brodys chowing down on some "recycled" corn in a later meal. And here I thought grubs were the grossest thing someone could eat when playing Survivor.

As disgusting as it was, I do love hearing cast members tell these stories from Survivor 51 that we didn't see in the episodes. With only 90 minutes (including commercials) to tell the story each week, it's totally understandable that something like this would fall by the wayside. Had the tribe actually gone through it and done it, however, I would be upset if it was left on the cutting room floor.

Survivor continues on CBS on Wednesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. With the remaining cast formed under one tribe, I can't wait to see what new alliances are forged. I'm also so invested in trying to figure out who won this season, because I'm still not entirely sure who is getting the winner's edit.

#3713. 25 Hours With World Of Warcraft: Forever

World of WarcraftWorld of Warcraft: Forever

Here are some things I have done in the 25 hours I have played of World of Warcraft: Forever so far:

Sound awful? Well…maybe. When I think about how I could be spending that time finally weeding my garden, or doing all the real-life chores I keep putting off, yeah. Bit of a waste of time. Such a waste of time, in fact, that I have hardly even touched most of the new content in WoW: Forever. I did play the Skyborne in beta: their starting island is fine. A bit too modern-feeling for me, but fine. I’ve definitely encountered a few new quests mixed in here and there, and the aforementioned torch and sleeping bag missions were new as well (though I did the former in beta and the latter in Season of Discovery already). But I haven’t even touched the new dungeons. I’m months away (at my current pace) from the new raids. I’m not even a high enough level to check out the Riverlands yet. May as well be playing Classic, right?

But as I hike back and forth and up and down Azeroth, I tilt my camera around. That draw distance! I see Mt. Hyjal, misty, looming in the distance, waiting for me at max level. The sun rises and sets over plains and swamps. It filters through trees and fog. I /wave at the other travelers I meet on the road. I sit at campfires and chat with others who gather around. People buff me with their class’ spells when they see me, or resurrect me if they see my dead body so that I don’t have to struggle all the way back to it. One person yesterday finished a quest just as I was starting, and volunteered to stick around (wasting 20 more minutes of their own time) to help me finish too. Another time, the game’s layer system goofed while I was on a zeppelin and something like 200 of us all ran into Undercity at once, prompting humorous panic from the folks already inside. Today, myself and two others started an entire, lengthy conversation in our zone’s general chat while I was squeezing in some early morning fishing time, just by saying “Good morning” in hopes someone would say it back. It ended with someone telling us all silly, made-up stories about a warlock named Daniel.

Somehow, this time doesn’t feel like such a waste anymore. It’s…soothing, I think. The slowness, the friction. A lot of this was always present in WoW Classic, sure. But I think the little added touches in Foreverâthe extra quests for things like torches and sleeping bags, the campfires, the layering ensuring that my world is always packed with other peopleâare lending the experience some new magic that wasn’t there before. In the past, the slowness of Classic felt more like a product of the time we were in, because no one had streamlined MMORPGs to eliminate it yet. But Forever embraces that pace and leans into it as a design feature rather than a flaw, making those moments feel rewarding on purpose rather than on occasional accident. More often than ever, you’re put in positions where there’s nothing to do but say hello to other people and forge a brief connection, or to sit back and admire the way the new lighting plays on the ripples in the river. It’s WoW, but with mindfulness. And mindfulness is something I’ve been in desperate want of lately.

Given that, it’s been really, really hard for me to put World of Warcraft: Forever down, even in the face of another brilliant game launch happening simultaneously. In my brain, a task list has populated of things I want to do: a dozen or so quests, of course, plus that one extra quest I have to turn in on the other continent, and that sleeping bag scavenger hunt I’m in the middle of. I need to visit my class trainer back in Orgrimmar or Thunder Bluff here soon to learn some new skills, and also all the profession trainers, and also the bank. There are some dungeons I’d like to run soon. All of this backs up in my brain the same way my real-life chores list does, but with the distinguishing feature that I dread none of it. I am eager to take part in every aspect, even though over half of these will inevitably be time-consuming, even time-wasting affairs. I’ll get to level 60 eventually, but I’m in no hurry to do it. To my editors: I’m sorry I’m inevitably going to take so long with this review. But there are so many wonderful, pointless distractions between here and there, I can’t help but let myself be blissful and slightly bored for another 50 or more hours first.

#3712. Head Of GTA 6 Owner Reveals His Advice To Be Healthy, Fit, And Live A Long Time

Strauss Zelnick, the head of Rockstar Games owner Take-Two, is known for his dedication to health and fitness. In 2018, he published a book titled Becoming Ageless: The Four Secrets To Looking and Feeling Younger Than Ever, and images of the executive looking shredded and lean at 8% body fat have circulated online. Zelnick has now spoken more about his health and fitness lifestyle, and offered some advice for people who want to get in shape and feel better.

Zelnick started off by telling Business Insider that he's good friends with Bryan Johnson, the billionaire who is trying to live forever, but Zelnick doesn't subscribe to the kinds of things Johnson is trying to do in terms of longevity in that regard.

Instead, Zelnick said he got some advice from his former doctor, the celebrity longevity doctor Peter Attia who appeared in the Epstein files, who told him he could help him with his healthspan but not his lifespan, and Zelnick was into that.

In 2016, Zelnick filmed a video for Business Insider where he showed off his workout routine--you can see it below.

Zelnick said his No. 1 piece of advice for anyone trying to improve their health is to avoid smoking altogether. "Smoking is the factor most highly correlated with a short, unhealthy, and frankly unhappy life. Don't smoke." Second, Zelnick said people should not abuse alcohol and drugs. "Those are the two most highly correlated factors with a bad old age, or no old age," he said.

After that, Zelnick said it's a good idea to get "some exercise," and that could be walking for 30 minutes four or five days a week. Zelnick said he goes way beyond this because health and fitness are his hobbies "but you really don't need to do that." Beyond exercise, Zelnick said he recommends that people eat a "responsible" diet, but it doesn't have to be "insanely healthy." The best practice for food, Zelnick said, is to simply not overdo it on unhealthy foods.

Another part of increasing your healthspan is getting enough sleep, and that should be about seven hours each night, Zelnick said. "If you're getting less than six hours of sleep a night, you're making bad decisions; that's what the math says," he said. "You are going to make bad personal decisions and bad professional decisions."

Having some kind of "emotional or spiritual life" is important, too, Zelnick said. "You have to have people you love and love you in your life, and preferably, you have to have a community around you," he said.

Also in the interview, Zelnick pushed back against taking peptides, which are popular in some fitness circles, but are largely unregulated.

"No. We have an FDA for a reason," he said. "Don't take something that is not double-blind tested. Even if it worked, do the stuff I do, forget the peptides, and you'll be in a better place."

Lastly, Zelnick said if people want to lose weight, they should consider taking some kind of GLP-1.

"Don't be grossly overweight. But in the world of GLP-1s, you have no reason to be," he said. "I am a huge advocate [for GLP-1s]. And no, there is absolutely no shame in taking them, whatsoever. If you're carrying extra weight, take a GLP-1. I happen never to have struggled with my weight, ever; I am blessed that way."

"I have this workout group, and I've had people show up who are heavyset, because we welcome everyone. So one guy shows up and he comes over and he says, 'I want you to talk to me about your diet, because I want to lost weight. I want to lose 50 pounds.' So I said, 'See, there are these things called GLP-1s. Go to my endocrinologist and get a prescription.' He said, 'Really? What about diet?' I said, 'That is literally like saying to me, I have a migraine, and I would say to you, forget about Tylenol, just meditate.' You take prescribed medications to help you live a healthier life. Of course."

#3711. Russell Brand's Ex Jemima Goldsmith Accuses Actor of Abuse After Sentencing

Russell Brand‘s ex-girlfriend Jemima Goldsmith is speaking out after the disgraced comedian was sentenced following his multiple convictions for rape and sexual assault.

“Firstly, and most importantly, I am and have always been strongly and unequivocally on the side of all of Brand’s victims,” Goldsmith, 52, wrote via X on Monday, November 9. “I am in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand’s trial, told their stories, testified and ensured justice was done. I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.”

Goldsmith — who dated Brand, 51, for roughly a year around 2014 — claimed that she was once forced to contact police to have him removed from her home during an alleged “violence incident.”

“I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children,” she claimed. “I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact.”

Goldsmith’s allegations came hours after Brand appeared in a London court on Monday and was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison after a jury found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Victim impact statements were read in court from the four women who came forward to report Brand’s crimes.

Russell previously entered a not guilty plea before he was tried on the seven sexual offense charges, all of which he denied. (The actor was found guilty on four of the seven counts.)

According to Goldsmith, she has assisted the journalists who helped expose the allegations against Brand and was willing to testify to his “abusiveness” in the event they were sued.

“I have spent much of my professional career trying to support unfairly demonised and silenced women, such as Monica Lewinsky and defending free speech,” she added. “I am glad and relieved that Russell Brand has finally faced justice.”

Us has reached out to Brand’s attorney for comment.

The Metropolitan Police confirmed to Us on Monday that detectives are not done investigating the alleged actions of Brand.

“The Met’s investigation into allegations of rape made by two women remains ongoing,” a Met Police spokesperson said in a statement without identifying any of the alleged victims. “The suspect has previously been interviewed under caution in connection with the allegations.”

Anyone who wishes to speak to detectives or make a report can contact the investigation team by email at CSOU@met.police.uk.

If you have experienced sexual assault, call the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 for confidential support.

#3710. Scott Colom’s Mississippi Votes Are Still Rolling In—and So Are the Views on His Viral Campaign Ads

In an era when short-form-video political messaging reigns supreme, it might be a tiebreaker, and even kingmaker, in Mississippi’s Senate midterm race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom narrowly leads incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as ballots continue to be counted on Thursday, November 5.

On October 13, Colom’s campaign released an ad that opens with a clip from a televised February interview featuring Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer and former agriculture commissioner, responding to a question about rising beef prices by offering that Mississippians “have so many proteins to choose from.” The ad then cuts to a man grilling burgers. “Pick another protein?” he asks. “Sheee-it. I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad appears to have been made by content creator Ryan Sayles. Vanity Fair has reached out to Sayles as well as Colom’s campaign for comment.

The message, which highlighted the Colom campaign’s commitment to cost cutting, capitalized on Hyde-Smith’s gaffe to the tune of more than 2.8 million views between X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook within the first 36 hours, according to the Clarion-Ledger. Former president Barack Obama’s video endorsement emphasizing Colom’s “Christian faith,” released just a day earlier, earned just over 700,000 views on the platforms in nearly double the time.

Colom currently has the edge in the historically deep-red state: If elected, he would become the first Democratic Mississippi Senator in more than 40 years—as part of the blue wave that swept the 2026 midterms, in which Democrats seized back control of both the House and Senate from MAGA-era Republicans. In Mississippi, which President Trump won by roughly 20 points in 2024, Hyde-Smith was favored to win. That is, until mid-October, when one of Colom’s campaign ads went viral, turning the Southern enclave into a surprise battleground state.

The day before Halloween, Colom made waves when he paid tribute to the Oscar-winning Ryan Coogler film Sinners, casting himself and his twin brother, Andrew, as fictional twins Smoke and Stack Moore, both portrayed by Michael B. Jordan in the movie. The film, which was set in the 1932 Mississippi Delta, follows the Black brothers as they try to keep white vampires away from their juke joint. The ad, titled “Sinators,” and released by Colom on October 30 with the disclaimer that “this is a joke!” shows the two men guarding a door as a blonde woman, who seems to be a proxy for Hyde-Smith, tries to enter. Colom says the duo have to “hold her off until the sun rises on Election Day” in the ad, which garnered more than 380,000 views on X alone prior to the November 3 election, as reported by the Sun Herald. If Colom wins, he would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era (1865–1877). VF has reached out to Coogler for comment on Colom’s campaign ad.

Colom’s attention-grabbing content hasn’t come without controversy. During the campaign, the candidate was compelled to delete another ad that featured an artificial-intelligence-generated depiction of Hyde-Smith running away from reporters after the state attorney general Lynn Fitch threatened legal action against him. (Fitch, a Republican, helped support Texas’s lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results, and was also counsel for the petitioner on Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the case which ultimately overturned Roe v. Wade.)

Shortly before the release of the Sinners ad, but after the AI dustup, the Senate Majority PAC, the flagship super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on a broadcast TV and digital ad campaign for Colom. “It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement to The Hill.

Colom, a local prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, seeking her second full term in the Senate, had a past connection heading into this political stand-off. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for federal judge in 2023, citing his support for transgender rights and his having previously been boosted by a George Soros–linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press. Colom told ABC News this “has nothing to do with the run for me…. As a Christian, I forgive her. It’s about the people in Mississippi.”

Since Mississippi elections do not have an automatic recount process, the opponents face a potential legal challenge over the results of their Senate race, in which Colom holds a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith. Colom later echoed a similar sentiment. “It’s not about me. It’s about the people in Mississippi,” the smiling Colom told reporters while speaking to constituents at a local establishment on Thursday morning. “They decided to go in a new direction.”

#3709. GTA 6 Pre-Orders Are Coming In ‘Far In Excess’ Of What Take-Two Expected, Says CEO

There’s just over a week left before Grand Theft Auto 6‘s launch, and by all accounts it sounds like it’s going to be massive. It feels like GTA 6 is everywhere, and early reports have suggested that the $100 digital deluxe edition is outselling even the $80 regular version. Even the CEO of Rockstar owner Take-Two is saying he’s surprised by how well the game is selling already, claiming in the company’s quarterly earnings that its pre-orders are “tracking far above our initial expectations.”

Pre-order incentives have been plentiful in recent weeks, with Walmart offering a “surprise” of some sort, and a lot of free bonus content bundled in no matter where you buy it. Digital pre-loads begin tomorrow, but physical pre-orders are a code in a box, so you won’t be able to redeem it until the day of. Physical discs won’t be available at launch.

What’s more bonkers to me than a nebulous “exceeded expectations” on pre-orders is that GTA 5 is still selling roughly five million copies per quarter, reaching nearly 235 million copies sold in the last few months. I’ve been watching Take-Two’s earnings for years now, and I don’t think I can remember a time when GTA 5 wasn’t selling at least five million per quarter. But if there were a time for it to drop off, I’d say now would be it, given that a brand new game is coming out imminently. And yet! The franchise overall has sold nearly 480 million units.

Overall, it wasn’t aÂ greatÂ quarter for Take-Two, with net bookings down 18 percent year-over-year and net revenue down as well. Take-Two is reiterating its guidance for the year, though, of net bookings of $8 to $8.2 billion: an absolutely bonkers amount of money that can only be explained by a new GTA (net bookings were $6.72 billion last year, and $5.56 billion the year prior).

GTA 6 is, curiously, the only upcoming game in Take-Two’s pipeline that has a firm release date at the moment. 2K is preparing its slate of sports titles for next year, and Project ETHOS, BioShock, and Judas are all still in limbo. For now, everything (quite understandably) hangs on GTA 6.

#3708. Ratchet & Clank Game Shutting Down Before Ever Fully Launching

Sony Interactive Entertainment and French developer Oh BiBi have announced Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble, a phone and tablet game, is coming to a close before it was even released fully.

In a statement, the developers said the game's final update is coming today, November 6, and the game itself will be removed from digital stores on November 21, 2026.

No information was provided as to why Ranger Rumble is shutting down. The game soft-launched in 2025 in limited territories, and expanded to more markets, but it's no longer going ahead with a full global release.

People who already have the game installed can keep playing until May 1, 2027, which is when the game's servers permanently close. Once the servers are shut down, the game will be completely unplayable.

Ranger Rumble is described as a "fast-paced multiplayer platformer arena shooter" where you battle others on a quest to become a galactic ranger.

In-app purchases have been removed from Ranger Rumble, and if you have a balance of currency, you should spend it before May 1, 2027. Alternatively, you can seek a refund from Apple’s App Store or Google Play.

"On behalf of the dev team and everyone helping to make the game, thanks to our amazing community for all your support, especially to those who have spent time playing, sharing feedback, and helping shape Ranger Rumble throughout its development," the developer said.

The latest entry in the mainline Ratchet & Clank series was 2021's Rift Apart. Its developer, Insomniac Games, has focused on Marvel properties more recently, releasing Marvel's Spider-Man 2 in 2023 and Marvel's Wolverine this year.

#3706. NBA 2K27 Sold Less Than Expected Because Of…GTA 6

Take-Two Interactive is one of the very few companies that, when selling four million units of something, can still get up and say that this was below forecast somehow. This was the case with NBA 2K27 upon its launch last quarter. And according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, one major reason for it missing internal expectation was…GTA 6.

In an interview with IGN, Zelnick was asked why NBA 2K27 came in below expectations as reported in the company’s quarterly earnings today. In response, Zelnick said the following:

I think the key point is that while below our forecast, NBA 2K27 is our second best release of NBA 2K in history. Itâs an immensely successful title. It sold 4 million units. And in launching more content than ever before for the rest of the year, we have expectations that the title will do even better than it already has done. I do think that this timing may have affected performance so far. It has been a crowded period, and we do think that GTA 6 coming has had an influence on the consumer. That said, weâre thrilled with how NBA 2K27 is performing.

The superhero genre is wildly popular, and fans who spent years watching the Marvel movies in order were shook when Guardians of the Galaxy director James Gunn pivoted to DC as the co-CEO of the studio. It's only been four years since he took the job and kickstarted the new DCU, but he and Peter Safran have already been replaced. I knew the Warner Bros. merger was going to result in some changes, but I didn't see this coming.

For the past few years, Gunn has been methodically crafting the new DCU, both in theaters and streaming with a HBO Max subscription. While the first few projects from Gods and Monsters have been released, a new report by THR claims that Gunn and Safran are stepping down as co-CEOS ,and being replaced former Marvel exec Jeremy Latcham. Talk about a change in leadership.

James Gunn took to Instagram to share his own response after this news broke, shocking superhero fans. His statement starts:

Thanks to all of you who have supported me and Peter in our time as the heads of DC Studios. When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri I used to write an draw my own comics with a mix of DC comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn't know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn't pass up the unique opportunity. I'm glad I took the job.

Per THR, Safran and Gun will end their time at co-CEOS of DC Studios on December 1st. Their four years at the studio resulted in the formation of a new shared universe, and the release of movie titles Superman, Supergirl, and Clayface, as well as TV shows Creature Commandos, Peacemaker, and Lanterns. Gunn is also directing Man of Tomorrow, which is expected to hit theaters next summer. Later in the director/writer/producer's statement on IG he got real about his time at the head of the studio, posting:

But what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the last. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that.) I'm always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to short breaks to unwind, and I've stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.

Gunn admits that he'll miss being the warden of the DCU, but also seems excited to go back to filmmaking rather than running the entire studio. In addition to bringing Man of Tomorrow to theaters, he's also a producer on The Batman: Part II and the forthcoming TV series The People v. Gorilla Grodd. Neither Gunn nor the report by THR give one specific reason for this change of the guard, but it certainly sounds like the Suicide Squad director is happy to be back behind the camera, rather than in a board rom.

You can see James Gunn's full statement about leaving his gig as co-CEO of DC Studios below:

Gunn's comments about missing his loved ones in some ways echoes what his wife Jennifer Holland told CinemaBlend earlier this year. Namely that he puts loved ones in his projects so he doesn't have to spend as much time away from them.

There are a few factors that might have gone into this decision. To start, there's Warner Bros.' merger with Paramount, which will likely influence a number of staffing changes for the newly formed company the Skydance Corporation. The DCU has also had a few missteps as of late. Supergirl struggled at the box office, while Lanterns was the subject of some backlash. The newest movie venture Clayface took #1 at the box office, but some people were disappointed it didn't have any real connections to Batman or the greater shared universe.

We'll just have to see how the new leadership affects the DCU as a whole, and the original plans for the shared universe. The next upcoming DC movie hitting theaters will be Man of Tomorrow, hitting theaters July 9th, 2027.
