#3637. DC Studios Shakeup: James Gunn And Peter Safran Out, Marvel Veteran Jeremy Latcham Taking Over

Today brings the stunning end of an era for DC Studios — yes, another one. Only four years after James Gunn and Peter Safran were brought on board to shepherd a rebooted DC Universe on the big and small screens, both creative heads are officially out and former Marvel Cinematic Universe creative Jeremy Latcham is in as their replacement. The news comes straight from the top of the newly-merged Skydance corporation, which has taken over ownership of the DC franchise following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. In an official release, Skydance chairman and CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz had this to say:

"James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we're incredibly proud of. We're grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand."

"Shocking" doesn't even begin to cover this turn of events, which comes only weeks after Gunn and Safran indicated Ellison appeared to be in favor of keeping both on board following the studio merger (via The Hollywood Reporter). Obviously, things have changed quite dramatically since then, with Ellison now pivoting to new leadership. Latcham may be familiar to Marvel fans as the former executive who produced several early films in the Marvel Cinematic Universe under Kevin Feige's leadership. Now, he'll get his chance at the top job as the newly-installed President and Chief Creative Officer of DC Studios ... even as several questions remain unanswered.

If it seems like the only consistency over at DC has been inconsistency over the last several years, you're not wrong! Ever since Zack Snyder was installed as the creative lead with "Man of Steel" in 2013, Marvel's distinguished competition has been beset by creative shakeups and overhauls ever since. Snyder gave way to a revolving door of several individual directors adding onto the then-DC Extended Universe, a brief (and bizarre) fling with Dwayne Johnson, an Elseworlds pivot with Todd Phillips' two "Joker" films and Matt Reeves' "The Batman," and most recently James Gunn and Peter Safran's unified take on the DC Universe.

Now, ex-Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham will be the next one on the hot seat ... and, at this point, it's unclear if DC will now undergo yet another top-to-bottom reboot under Skydance. That would be more than a bit awkward with Gunn's "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow" still slated to release next year, more DC movies to come afterwards, and even multiple shows currently in development (including a "Poison Ivy"-focused series). Could Latcham simply guide the next batch of movies and shows to come, keeping everything in a loose continuity with the foundation Gunn and Safran established? The biggest hint might be found in the joint statement by David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz:

"Jeremy has been a longtime creative partner to both, and we have complete confidence that James and Peter will ensure a smooth, collaborative transition and continue this work with care. We look forward to working with Jeremy to build the next generation of DC storytelling and to doubling down on our commitment to fans."

Stay tuned to /FIlm as we wait and see how Latcham's DC will ultimately take shape.

#3635. Kate Middleton, Prince William, King Charles, and Queen Camilla Gather For Remembrance Day

This Sunday, November 8, King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Kate Middleton, Prince William, Princess Anne and other members of the royal family came together to observe Remembrance Sunday, one of the most solemn events on the United Kingdom's calendar. The day marks the anniversary of the armistice that ended World War I, signed on “the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month” in 1918.

The focal point of every Remembrance Day is the Cenotaph in Whitehall, the Portland stone monument where tribute is paid to those who fell in the wars and conflicts in which the country has participated. Every year, representatives of the royal family, political leaders, the Armed Forces, and veterans gather there: This year, more than 10,000 marched alongside the king and the prime minister.

True to tradition, Charles III laid a wreath at the memorial on behalf of the nation and led the royal family. At his side was Prince William, Princess Anne, and the Duke of Edinburgh, who also paid their respects with a floral tribute. Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales, Kate Middleton, watched the ceremony from the balcony of the Foreign Office, as is customary. On the political front, Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath on his first Remembrance Sunday as head of the government, accompanied by Opposition Leader Kemi Badenoch and other political leaders.

The day before had already been a day of remembrance: the King, the Queen, and the Princes of Wales attended the Festival of Remembrance at the Royal Albert Hall, the major tribute to the armed forces that precedes Remembrance Sunday.

#3634. Superman Director James Gunn Explains Departure As DC Studios Co-Head

When the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merger was completed a little over a month ago, questions about the direction of the newly-established mega company Skydance, the formation of which required massive investments from Elon Musk, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi, were myriad. For moviegoers, one of the biggest concerns was the future of the DC Universe. Co-executives James Gunn and Peter Safran had been at the helm for four years, and the results were mixed. Gunn's "Superman" was a blockbuster, while "Peacemaker," "Creature Commandos," "Lanterns," and "Clayface" were popular with fans. They stumbled badly with Craig Gillespie's critical and commercial flop "Supergirl," but a course correction seemed to be on the horizon with the Man of Steel sequel "Man of Tomorrow."

Evidently, something or someone changed Ellison's mind over the last month because Gunn and Safran are out. It's a stunning reversal of fortune for the duo, but at least Gunn and Safran had time to write this statement:

"Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore Superman to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with 'Peacemaker,' 'Creature Commandos,' 'Lanterns,' and 'Clayface.' We're immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews, and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We've shared a creative history with [new DC Studios head] Jeremy [Latcham] going back to Marvel, and we're eager to see the perspective he brings to DC's next chapter. We're excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex's journey in 'Man of Tomorrow.'"

James Gunn also took to Instagram to issue his own statement. He thanked fans for their support, adding:

"When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters. Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream come true. I didn't know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn't pass up the unique opportunity. I'm glad I took the job."

Yet, despite the "highs" of "Superman," "Clayface," and the upcoming "The People vs. Gorilla Grodd" and "Man of Tomorrow" (which he called "the best experience of my life"), Gunn admitted that he disliked "the at-times corporate nature of the job." He then apologized to his wife Jennifer Holland for being preoccupied with the massively demanding gig of being a filmmaker and a studio executive, explaining:

"And the thing my ADHD hyperfocus has had the most difficulty with has been dividing my time between projects I'm incredibly passionate about and the ones I'm not so much and all the things I have to do as a studio head."

Maybe that's why he didn't mention "Supergirl" in either statement? Anyway, Gunn closed out his statement by saying he's excited to get back to "pure filmmaking," which suggests to me that he's eager to make a non-superhero movie for the first time since 2006's gleefully gross alien horror comedy "Slither." (Admittedly, Gunn's 2010 film "Super" wasn't a traditional superhero movie, but it was a riff on the genre.) I wish him the best, and congratulate him for not having to work for David Ellison much longer.

We can all agree that the Olaf animatronic walking itself around Disneyland Paris is adorable, all on its own. Now it's even cuter, with his own magical sleigh to help transport him around the Kingdom of Arendelle as he makes his way to a stage where the Arendelle Carolers perform for the holidays.

One of the biggest drawbacks that came with introducing a “living” animatronic Olaf to guests in Disney’s European theme park is the fact that it can’t walk very far very quickly. I mean, he is a snowman after all. So now, and just in time for the holiday celebration, the adorable snowman who just wants to live his best summer is taking on winter in style with his own magical sleigh. Check out the short clip of a cast member steering Olaf around as he waves to the adoring masses gathered around:

A post shared by EveryCharacter.com (@everycharacter)

The holidays are in full swing in the Disney theme parks around the world, and no one embodies the winter season better than Olaf the snowman from Frozen, one of Walt Disney Animation Studios’ most popular franchises of all time. As a result, I’m happy to see that the beloved character has his own mode of transportation, especially after a few incidents of Olaf failing, freezing, and falling over. It’s a frightening sight when it happens, though Josh Gad has kept a sense of humor about it all, as the actor who is responsible for the snowman's lovable personality.

Getting to meet beloved Disney characters is a longtime tradition, where animated characters become live-action characters in the parks. While we knew that Disney Parks had been working on robots for a few years, it wasn’t until we actually got to see Olaf in action that I realized just how remarkable the achievement was. I’m also thankful that they’re continuing to build on that by creating this sleigh, which seems to have a purpose bigger than just transporting the character around the World of Frozen in Disneyland Paris.

In the video clip, you can see that Olaf’s sleigh, while too freaking cute just on its own, has the dual purpose of also working as a bridge to get him onto the stage at the foot of North Mountain so that he can join the Arendelle carolers for a 15-minute musical performance where he leads the choir. The sleigh transforms into a short platform that Olaf can shuffle across to the back of the stage where he can do his part in the show, avoiding the need for someone to have to physically lift him up and get him on the stage some other way.

While more Frozen films are in the works, we won’t see Frozen 3 until November 24, 2027. Until then, I’m hoping we’ll get more Olaf fun in and around the Disney theme parks, as he’s a character that would be a welcome addition to the U.S. locations as well.

#3631. How Original Narnia Star Ben Barnes Really Feels About Netflix's Reboot

We are a couple of months away from Greta Gerwig unleashing her take on the fantasy classic "The Magician's Nephew" for Netflix and a new generation of kids experiencing the world of Narnia for the first time. The film is already making some interesting choices when it comes to adapting the magical world created by author C. S. Lewis, including assembling a killer cast that features Meryl Streep as the lion Aslan and Daniel Craig as the titular magician.

So, since we're waiting for its arrival, it's never a bad time to revisit the previous big-budget movie adaptations of Lewis' fantasy novels. After all, for a certain generation, "Shrek" director Andrew Adamson's film versions of the "Narnia" books were their introduction to fantasy (and to the isekai genre that's come to dominate anime). Indeed, if you were too young to watch Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" movie trilogy in theaters in the 2000s, chances are Adamson's films were the first big-screen fantasy epics you saw (you know, assuming you were alive back then). It makes sense, too, as Wētā Workshop worked on those movies, designing incredible fantastical creatures and props.

Adamson's "Narnia" films also featured a number of actors who have gone on to become bigger names, including James McAvoy and Ben Barnes as Prince Caspian (a role he later reprised in the Michael Apted-helmed "The Voyage of the Dawn Treader"). Now, Barnes shared his feelings about the Netflix "Narnia" reboot, telling ScreenRant that "the trailer looks great" and that he's "always been a fan of directors who are real visionaries."

Ben Barnes went on to praise the decision to start with "The Magician's Nephew" for Netflix's reboot of the "Narnia" movie franchise, saying it's a "brilliant idea."

"I think [Greta Gerwig} has got a great eye for casting. I loved Emma Mackey in 'Sex Education,' I thought she was brilliant. Obviously, Daniel Craig's brilliant in everything. So, yeah, I'm really excited to see it," Barnes added. "Those stories are beautiful, but also, every generation needs to reinterpret things, and pull out of stories what seems visceral and important, and present it in a way that is visually exciting, and I think we can rely on [Gerwig] to do that."

From what we know about the movie, it seems Gerwig is embracing a '70s glam rock and British prog musical sensibility for her take on "Narnia," including giving Aslan a David Bowie-inspired look. That alone makes this a rather interesting adaptation. But most importantly, it is a huge risk for Netflix, between the film's daunting budget and Gerwig's desire for a wide theatrical release leading to some behind-the-scenes drama.

Admittedly, it's a bummer that audiences never got to see Barnes appear in more "Narnia" movies. At the same time, he did go on to join another popular fantasy franchise in the form of Netflix's "Shadow and Bone" TV series (even though it wound up being canceled before its story was completed). As for "The Magician's Nephew," we'll see how Gerwig's take on Narnia fares with the masses when it opens in theaters (including IMAX screens) on February 12, 2027, before debuting on Netflix a couple of months later on April 2.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Those numbers line up with what you’d expect from a unit this size, and they make it useful for both emergencies and planned outdoor use.

You also get a solid mix of ports—there are three AC outlets, a 30-amp port for heavier appliances or RV setups, multiple USB-C ports (including a 140W option for laptops), and DJI’s own SDC ports for direct drone charging. If you use DJI gear, that alone makes life easier in the field, notes this Mashable review. Recharging is also fast for a battery this size. Plugged into a wall outlet, it can go from empty to full in about 90 minutes. You can also top it up with solar panels or from your car, which makes it workable for longer trips. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Note that this unit has no built-in light, which is something many competing power stations include.

An era in superhero-related media is officially coming to an end, as James Gunn and Peter Safran are officially stepping down from their posts as the co-CEOs of DC Studios. This surprising news arrives only a few weeks after the finalization of the Paramount/Warner Bros. merger. At this point, the news is still very fresh and, based on social media, the responses to this major development vary tremendously. Interestingly enough, amid all that, one fan brought up a wild fact regarding Gunn’s tenure, and I’m feeling so many emotions.

Gunn and Safran joined DC Studios in 2022 and, from there, they began to construct their DCU continuity, which was to span movies, TV and video games. The pair eventually developed a ten-year plan and, up to this point, that strategy has yielded films like Superman and Supergirl as well as shows like Creature Commandos and Lanterns. The wild comment that was recently shared by an X user had nothing to do with any projects like that, though. Instead, they marked the end of this chapter by naming a long-gestating flick:

Very funny/sad that the entire Gunn era took place between THE BATMAN and THE BATMAN PART 2.

I’m honestly at a loss for words here, as this fact is absolutely correct. Matt Reeves’ The Batman was released in March 2022 months before Safran and Gunn were hired. The sequel was announced in April of that year and, since then, the movie has seen a variety of delays and is currently set to hit theaters in early 2028. On the one hand, it’s understandable that someone would chuckle over the fact that this sequel’s development will have outlasted the Gunn/Safran era. But, on the other hand, I’m actually a bit sad.

James Gunn Doesn’t Hold Back About Rumors Swirling Around Man Of Tomorrow And More DC Projects

As someone who has been interested in the DCU thus far, I’m a bit disappointed over the possibility of another reboot. However, what really makes me sad about the fact pointed out in the social media is that it’s a reminder of just how long The Batman: Part II’s development has taken. Of course, I do understand the reasons, though, as the Hollywood strikes played a key role in that. Also, more recently, Reeves had to take a step back from the film to handle a personal matter, and Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to complete principal photography. Reeves isn’t leaving the movie entirely, though, as he'll remain in touch with Soderbergh during the shoot and completely retake the reins during post-production.

It was just weeks ago that Reeves’ situation was announced and it was mentioned that he had support from Safran and Gunn. That’s just one detail that makes the news of their departure all the more surreal to me. Gunn posted about his exit on his Instagram and reflected on the highs of working for DC. Additionally, the filmmaker praised the various collaborators he had the chance to work with. Overall, Gunn – a longtime fan of DC Comics – seems to have a lot of gratitude for his time serving as co-CEO of the studio.

While James Gunn and Peter Safran will vacate their positions ahead of Jeremy Latcham’s arrival by December 1, their work within the DCU isn’t done just yet as, at the very least, he’s still in post-production on his Superman follow-up, Man of Tomorrow, which is set to be released amid the 2027 movie schedule. Also, Gunn and Safran are still credited as producers on The Batman’s sequel. I’m not sure what lies ahead for DC but, for now, I’m going to be glued to my screen to see if any other fans drop any other wild facts.

Man of Tomorrow soars into theaters on July 9, 2027, while The Batman: Part II opens on February 18, 2028.

#3628. Denzel Washington's Gritty Sci-Fi Western Movie Is Worth Revisiting

The Hughes Brothers' 2010 sci-fi Western film "The Book of Eli" stars Denzel Washington as the titular Eli, a machete-wielding rogue who wanders a post-apocalyptic Earth years after a nuclear holocaust has laid waste to vast swaths of the planet's surface. It's not so far in the future that Eli doesn't still have a working mp3 player, though, and he barters things in exchange for battery charges at the occasional mercantile outpost.

Eventually, Eli runs afoul of Carnegie (Gary Oldman), an aspiring post-apocalyptic warlord who is looking for a legendary book, believing it will allow him to take control of the populace. Three guesses as to which book he's looking for.

"The Book of Eli" is pretty badass, with a chalky, dusty aesthetic that's unique in the annals of post-apocalyptic thrillers. Washington, one of the best actors of his generation, gives Eli a soulful humanity while also making him a capable action hero, able to take down teams of attackers with his sword. (He even fights off a guy with a chainsaw in one scene.) And while critics weren't super-high on the film, it was something of a hit, enough so for a "Book of Eli" prequel series to enter development in 2024.

The movie's supporting cast is impressive as well. Mila Kunis, for example, plays Carnegie's daughter Solara, who is unsavorily ordered to seduce Eli when he comes into her father's field of vision. What's more, Tom Waits has a small part as a shop owner, Jennifer Beals plays Carnegie's mistress, Michael Gambon and Frances de la Tour show up as a pair of itinerant cannibals, and Malcolm McDowell has an uncredited role as a much more friendly book collector.

If you don't know the various twists in "The Book of Eli," I would recommend you watch the movie before looking up any plot synopses. There are several notable, fun reveals, especially at the film's end, that should not be spoiled. The one thing I will mention is that Carnegie is, in fact, on the hunt for a Bible. Religion appears to have fallen by the wayside in the movie's dusty wastelands, and Carnegie, while not a believer, seems to know that Christianity can be wielded as a cudgel to control the masses. Indeed, all known Bibles had been destroyed following the global nuclear strike.

It's a pretty damning, almost anti-religious theme, when you think about it. The only legacy that Christianity will bring into the future is the way it was wielded by political leaders as a means to sway votes. Eli, meanwhile, has a much more righteous grasp of the Bible, understanding its philosophies and cultural impact more profoundly. "The Book of Eli" explores themes of God and godlessness in desperate times, its central conflict being a wholly Christian idea of faith vs. ambition. Despite its violence and badassery, one could imagine "The Book of Eli" being shown as the warm-up movie in a Bible study course.

The Hughes Brothers burst onto the scene in 1993 with their crime drama "Menace II Society" before helming other impressive films like "Dead Presidents," the documentary "American Pimp," and the Jack the Ripper film "From Hell," based on a comic by Alan Moore. After "The Book of Eli," the siblings went their separate ways creatively, with Allen Hughes helming the 2013 thriller "Broken City" and the documentary miniseries "The Defiant Ones" and "Dear Mama." Albert Hughes, meanwhile, made the 2018 prehistoric actioner "Alpha." Together, they're responsible for some of the best action movies from Black directors of all time.

As mentioned, critics weren't terribly kind to "The Book of Eli," although several prominent reviewers were on its wavelength. Notably, Roger Ebert gave the film three stars (out of four), feeling that it starts out grim but falls into Western cliches in a way that makes the whole thing more watchable and even enjoyably silly. As he put it:

"[Denzel] Washington and the Hughes brothers do a good job of establishing this man and his world, and at first, 'The Book of Eli' seems destined to be solemn. But then Eli arrives at a Western town ruled by Carnegie, who, like all the local overloads in Westerns and gangster movies, sits behind a big desk flanked by a tall bald guy and, of course, a short scruffy one. How are these guys recruited? Wanted: Tall bald guy to stand behind town boss and be willing to sacrifice life. All the water you can drink."

Ebert added that the movie's ending is "flawed" yet "it's so magnificently, shamelessly, implausibly flawed" that it makes "The Book of Eli" stick in the memory for how gloriously implausible it is. That's not a negative thing.

#3627. LACMA Art+Film Gala: Nicole Kidman, Timothée Chalamet Honor Denis Villeneuve

“It’s a pleasure to be here. You guys are just crazy party people,” said artist Vija Celmins as she summed up the jovial atmosphere at the 15th annual LACMA Art+Film Gala during her casual and off-the-cuff acceptance speech as one of the two honorees that night.

The annual fundraiser is a party, and unique among the many galas that hit the town this time of year. Along with raising money for the museum’s initiative to make film more central to its programming (this year it raised a record-breaking almost $7 million), it brings out an eclectic mix of A-list talent, up-and-coming filmmakers, and giants of the art world.

Honoree, Denis Villeneuve, Honoree Vija Celmins, co-chair Eva Chow and LACMA CEO Michael Govan

Just a quick scan of the packed room: Al Pacino sitting with artist Ed Ruscha and art dealer Larry Gagosian; artist Alex Israel wrapping his arm around Orlando Bloom for a photo; model Alex Consani crouching down to chat with influencer and comedian Quenlin Blackwell; and artists Jonas Wood and Mickalene Thomas chatting in one corner while Sarah Paulson and Parker Posey catch up in another.

Anya Taylor-Joy set the mood for the evening as one of the first arrivals on the red carpet, where talent posed in front of Chris Burden’s famed public art installation Urban Light. There in support of Dune director Denis Villeneuve, who was honored along with Celmins, the Dune: Part Two star wore a vintage 1997 Pierre Cardin haute couture bridal gown with a sheer silver overlay that looked both of the past and of the future.

Villeneuve’s leading man, Timothée Chalamet, skipped the carpet altogether, instead slipping into the crowded tent for dinner in a seat next to Villeneuve and his wife, producer Tanya Lapointe. Chalamet arrived separately from girlfriend Kylie Jenner, who did walk the carpet in a low-back Ashi Studio gown. When Jenner arrived at her table, she was seated opposite Chalamet, reaching across to grab his hand.

Seated next to Villeneuve was Nicole Kidman (in a voluminous, ballerina-inspired Chanel dress), who flew 15 hours from Australia to give Villeneuve his award. “The truth is I’ve never really met Denis. I’ve met him on some red carpets and sort of waved at him,” she said during her remarks. “Yet somehow I feel like I know the deepest parts of him because that is what extraordinary filmmakers do. They let you in. They reveal themselves to us through their work. They invite you into their imaginations, into their dreams, into their questions, and into their fears.”

Monica Barbaro, Salma Hayek and Kim Kardashian

Before Villeneuve took the stage, a video capturing his film legacy of big, bold, and personal epics like Sicario, Blade Runner 2049, Arrival, and the Dune trilogy was played, featuring a slew of A-list directors singing his praises, including Steven Spielberg, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, James Cameron, and Chloé Zhao. “I’ve always felt that cinema is seen as a Pop art—the film carries the burden of being popular in the present,” said Villeneuve in his acceptance speech. “But at the end of the day, the real challenge is to make something that can enter the test of time.”

Speaking of tests (screen tests, that is) Villeneuve got a bit playful with the end of his speech, announcing to the room that he would—right here, right now—announce which actor would play James Bond. The French Canadian director is helming the next Bond film, and over the past week reports have been flying about who might be cast. Would Villeneuve put us all out of our misery and spill the beans? “The actor who will play the next James Bond is—and I will stop right now because [producer] Amy Pascal is about to have a heart attack,” he said with a smile.

The gala, once again presented by Gucci, hosted a slew of this Oscar season’s most exciting young filmmakers, including Obsession filmmaker Curry Barker and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, along with La Bola Negra directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known as Los Javis). The latter told me they didn’t plan to party as hard as they did at the Academy Museum Gala a few weeks ago, where they went viral for singing along to Taylor Swift’s performance of “Love Story.” Said Ambrossi, “I’m drinking only water tonight.”

Among the other guests, Joel Edgerton chatted with Abbott Elementary’s Quinta Brunson and Daniel Scheinert, one half of the Oscar-winning directing team Daniels (Everything Everywhere All at Once). Kim Kardashian wove her way through the crowd, pausing perfectly to look over her shoulder for a trailing photographer. And several stars made a date night out of the event: Sienna Miller brought fiancé Oli Green; Julia Garner sat with musician Charlie Walker; Viola Davis enjoyed the night with husband and producing partner Julius Tennon. Paris Hilton, who introduced Rosé onstage with her classic catchphrase “that’s hot,” wore a glittering Jenny Packham gown as she cascaded through the room with her husband, Carter Reum.

Eva Chow, who had co-chaired the gala for the past 15 years with Leonardo DiCaprio, announced that she’d be stepping down from her post after this year. Dubbed the “Culture Queen of Los Angeles,” she is credited with bringing together Hollywood and the art world for the event, helping grow it into the must-attend party of the season. DiCaprio couldn’t make it this year because he has a cold, but his girlfriend, model Vittoria Ceretti, was there to represent him.

But with all these big Hollywood types in the room, it was Celmins who stole the show—though she didn’t mean to. In a video that ran before her acceptance speech, the artist welcomed the video crew into her home, revealing her quick-witted humor, her ornery cat (she claims to be a dog person), and her love of Bob Dylan. Celmins is best known for her boundless work inspired by nature, including ocean waves, desert floors, and starry night skies. She charmed the crowd with her boundless personality as well.

LACMA had plenty to celebrate this year too. After a 20-year-long planning and development process, the David Geffen Galleries were completed this past year. As partygoers entered the tent for dinner, the silhouette of the formidable new building stood out in the background. “Same tent. Different buildings around it,” joked LACMA CEO Michael Govan during his opening remarks.

After his speech, Villeneuve and all the guests made their way out to LACMA’s main courtyard, where Rosé would perform under the stars. I joked with him that I thought he would make some news with that tease of a Bond casting, and then wondered if he likes being the center of attention at a gala like this. He said he values the connections he makes with other filmmakers and artists at these events. “I like talking one-on-one,” he said.

Noor Alfallah, Al Pacino, Erica Pelosini, Larry Gagosian and Ed Ruscha

While Rosé performed four songs for the black-tie-clad audience, Emily in Paris star Ashley Park and In the Heights actor Anthony Ramos swayed to her ballad “Number One Girl.” Popcorn and cotton candy were passed out to the audience, which, naturally, sang along when Rosé ended her set with her biggest hit, “APT.” Andrew Garfield led his Artificial costar Monica Barbaro by the hand through the crowd. Though the pair didn’t pose for photos on the carpet together, the couple (who have been romantically linked since 2025) spent the evening in close contact as they chatted with friends like Salma Hayek Pinault.

Villeneuve’s speech best captured the evening’s one-of-a-kind mash-up of art and film when he spoke passionately about the importance of human effort in the era of AI. “I can create something with a prompt, or I can go into the desert with actors, with a crew, and go on a real adventure where I learn about life and become better at my craft,” he said. “More important than the result is the process. The process is how the human experience acquires its meaning. In this moment in time, it is more important than ever that human beings keep making art together.”

Odessa A'zion in a Charles & Ron + Maison Privee coat.

#3625. 10 Funniest 'Far Side' Comics About Dinosaurs That Prove Gary Larson Is a Mad Genius

On May 27, 1982, The Far Side cartoonist Gary Larson published what would become one of the most famous comic strips ever. The image features a classroom full of cavemen being taught by a caveman instructor, and the instructor points at an image of a Stegosaurus tail, specifically the spiky thing at the bottom of the tail. Larson's caption reads, “Now, this end is called the thagomizer … after the late Thag Simmons.”

On the surface, this might not seem like such a big deal. It's just one more of Larson’s many silly comic strips featuring cavemen. But this one ended up taking on a life of its own.

At the time this comic was published, that spiky apparatus at the end of a Stegosaurus’ tail actually had no name at all. So scientists began to jokingly use the word “thagomizer” to describe it. Eventually, the usage became so common that it came to be scientifically recognized and used by such distinguished institutions as the Smithsonian, confirming that one little Far Side joke made scientific dinosaur history.

But while that comic may be Larson’s most famous and historically significant dinosaur comic strip, it was far from his only one. Larson regularly drew dinosaurs in his cartoons, oftentimes doing normal human things or being completely unaware of their impending extinction. The Far Side ran from 1980 until 1995 and Larson created over 4,000 strips during that time. Dozens of them featured dinosaurs. And while only one made dinosaur history, there have been lots of unforgettable ones for Far Side fans. Here are 10 of the most unforgettable Far Side comics about dinosaurs (besides the thagomizer one).

Larson regularly depicted dinosaurs as doing normal human stuff, and the comedy came from these giant prehistoric monsters acting so calmly. Like this one, there’s nothing that funny about flossing, but when a T-rex talks about it, it’s hilarious.

This strip, about a juvenile T-rex looking for the prize in the bottom of a cereal box, is another one with dinosaurs acting like humans. The comedy is only enhanced here by the writing on the box, “Free kid inside!”

Here, Larson depicts a dinosaur press conference where one dinosaur declares that the climate is changing and mammals are taking over. It’s a really clear example of Larson’s other big dinosaur theme: extinction. A lot of Far Side comics are incredibly dark in their humor, and with dinosaurs, Larson seemed to love depicting them as doomed creatures, usually with no idea that their destruction is imminent.

In this woman’s defense, that does look a lot like a dryer.

This one, from August 9, 1985, is a bit of a play on the difficulty people have with dinosaur names. As a dinosaur nerd, though, I feel compelled to say that pterosaurs, like the one pictured here, are not dinosaurs. They are a completely separate group of reptiles which existed at the same time as dinosaurs, but are not dinosaurs themselves. Technically, it would be more accurate to put a comic strip featuring a chicken on this list, as birds are dinosaurs (and Larson did a ton of chicken comics).

Okay, I’ll add one chicken comic to this list, only because it’s also a dinosaur comic (and again, birds are dinosaurs).

Again, pterosaurs aren’t dinosaurs, but this joke, from January 18, 1986, is too funny to resist. It becomes all the funnier when you take a look at the limbs of the caveman in the back.

Some of Larson’s best dinosaur jokes are actually about the paleontologists, like this one. While people might expect paleontologists to be dull, sober scientists, Larson loved to depict them, and other scientists, as ridiculous children.

This is one of Larson’s best Far Side comics without any words. The visual of dinosaurs as schoolyard bullies, picking on a mammal for its fur, is funny enough, but the dinosaur in the back, noticing that it's snowing, gives the comic levels. Again, it's Larson poking fun at dinosaurs who have no idea their days are numbered.

Aside from the thagomizer comic, this has got to be Gary Larson’s most famous dinosaur image. From December 15, 1982, this absurd cartoon shows dinosaurs smoking cigarettes with the caption “The real reason dinosaurs became extinct.” The comic combines Larson’s two big dinosaur themes, in that it shows them doing normal human stuff and it’s about their extinction. It's also an image that is both smart and profoundly silly, like the very best Far Side comics.

#3624. 5 Reasons Why Godzilla Minus Zero Ruled The Box Office

The King of the Monsters is back on top of the box office. Director Takashhi Yamazaki's "Godzilla Minus Zero" stomped into theaters over the weekend and it made quite the impact. Given that "Godzilla Minus One" was officially the first movie in the franchise to win an Oscar, the pressure was on for the sequel. It's safe to say that Yamazaki delivered.

Released by Toho and GKIDS, "Godzilla Minus Zero" opened to $30.5 million domestically to go with $31.4 million internationally for a $61.9 million global debut. That's the biggest opening weekend ever for a live-action foreign-language movie in North America, topping Jet Li's "Hero" ($17.8 million). It's also the biggest global opening for a Japanese "Godzilla" movie. Since we're talking about a 72-year-old franchise, that's pretty darn good.

For context, "Minus One" opened to $11.4 million en route to $114 million worldwide. The fact that the sequel opened nearly three times higher is staggering. Yes, this movie carries a bigger budget, but bigger is relative. It's still believed to be in the $20 million range, which is hard to believe but makes this instantly profitable for all involved.

So, what went right here? How did Toho manage to turn this into a massive breakout sequel? How did Yamazaki manage to live up to such high expectations? We're going to look at the biggest reasons why "Godzilla Minus Zero" ruled the box office on its opening weekend. Let's get into it.

Having critics on a movie's side certainly never hurts. Having critics and audiences on a movie's side? That's when good things can really start to happen. And much like "Minus One" before it, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has proved to be a real crowd-pleaser through and through.

The sequel currently holds a stellar 90% critical approval rating to go with an outstanding 96% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. It also earned an A CinemaScore, which bodes very well for word of mouth in the coming weeks. A big opening weekend is one thing, but "Godzilla Minus One" became fall 2023's unexpected box office hero thanks to excellent legs driven by real-world buzz from moviegoers. It looks like something similar is in store this time around, only much bigger.

Takashi Yamazaki's follow-up takes place two years after the events of "Minus One," bringing back much of the same human cast. A new threat in the form of King Ghidorah emerges, plunging Japan into chaos once more, leading to an epic monster bash with Godzilla himself.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai said "Godzilla Minus Zero" is "bigger" and "badder" but "not quite better" in his review. Whether or not one necessarily thinks the sequel is better than its predecessor is a conversation for another time, but it at the very least appears to be satisfying the intended audience. Almost nobody seems to be leaving theaters disappointed. That matters more for the moment than how we, as a society, may ultimately rank these movies in the future.

"Godzilla" has been around as a franchise for more than 70 years. The big lizard is a truly enduring cinematic icon unlike any other. The past few years, in particular though, have been shockingly fruitful. We're truly living in the golden age of "Godzilla." This recent surge in the character's popularity has also brought a lot of new fans on board. In particular, the Japanese movies in the series have been opened up to a much wider audience thanks almost exclusively to "Godzilla Minus One."

This franchise contains multitudes. A lot of people grew up engaging with the Toho movies passively, perhaps seeing something like "Godzilla vs. Mothra" on TV. But "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever because it was, quite frankly, one of the greatest movies in the history of this cherished series. It was too good to be ignored and people who only passively engaged with the previous movies discovered something to love.

"Minus One" opened Western audiences up to Japanese "Godzilla" movies more than ever before. Yes, the MonsterVerse movies like "Godzilla vs. Kong" have been very successful in North America, but engagement with these Japanese-language entries is now happening on another, much larger level. The fact that "Godzilla Minus Zero" made nearly three times what its predecessor did on opening weekend speaks to that.

Come what may in the weeks andmonths ahead, there's no question that this movie's breakout success is a direct result of "Minus One" opening up this corner of the franchise to a much wider audience globally.

IMAX has proved that it's more important to the box office than ever before time and time again in recent years. Hollywood studios literally plan their biggest releases around the availability of those premium format screens because those higher ticket prices add a lot to the bottom line. Movies like Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and "Top Gun: Maverick," among many others, made a great deal of extra cash thanks to IMAX. The same can now be said for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

According to a press release, the sequel opened to $21.3 million worldwide on IMAX screens, representing the biggest IMAX global opening ever for a Japanese film. Even more impressive? IMAX screens delivered around 34% of the movie's global opening on less than 1% of total screens. Toho benefited greatly from those screens this time around.

But that's only part of the equation. "Minus Zero" earned the "must-see in theaters" label, becoming a true cinematic event. IMAX isn't the only game in town as far as premium formats go; 4DX, Cinemark XD, and Dolby Cinema screens were also packed out across North America and the rest of the world. Comparing Dolby Cinema to IMAX and how these formats differ isn't important to this conversation. All of these formats warrant higher ticket prices, which audiences were clearly happy to pay in this particular case. That played a big role in driving the record-breaking opening.

"Godzilla Minus One" benefited greatly from an early November release date, and "Godzilla Minus Zero" has arrived three years later in a similar spot on the calendar. GKIDS and Toho went with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" line of thinking with the scheduling, and it's tough to argue with the results. This was the absolute perfect spot on the calendar for this movie.

There is often a bit of a lull at the box office in early November. There's the post-Halloween horror hangover and studios are generally holding back their biggest, best stuff for the Thanksgiving corridor. "Minus Zero" opened against "The Cat in the Hat," which flopped with $20.5 million, and Angel's "Drummer Boy," which was non-threatening at $9.3 million. Looking ahead, "Ebenezer" may top the box office this upcoming weekend, but it's also going for a very different audience.

A big threat doesn't emerge until "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" on November 20, when "Godzilla" will already be three weekends in. Sure, once Thanksgiving arrives with "Focker In-Law" and Disney's "Hexed" both opening, competition will be more fierce but it's easy to see an R-rated monster movie still serving as solid counterprogramming throughout the entire month.

"Godzilla" has been broadly popular as a franchise ever since its inception. Like any long running franchise though, it's had some peaks and valleys. Right now? It's at an unquestioned peak. So much so that it's easy to make the argument that Godzilla is one of our most important modern movie stars. That may sound silly, but it's no less true.

In the 2020s, few real-life movie stars can compete with the King of the Monsters. Even in 2021 when theaters were on life support, "Godzilla vs. Kong" battled the pandemic and won, proving that blockbuster cinema could still exist. It's arguably one of the most important hits in recent history. That's just the tip of the iceberg though.

We've already mentioned that "Godzilla Minus One" became the biggest Japanese "Godzilla" movie ever, serving as a real shock at the time. Then, just a handful of months later, "Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire" became the highest-grossing "Godzilla" movie ever, pulling in more than $570 million worldwide.

"Godzilla x Kong" pushed the MonsterVerse past the $2 billion mark globally as well. We certainly have to give King Kong his flowers, but Godzilla has been remarkably consistent in the 2020s. Even the re-release of "Shin Godzilla" last year outperformed the movie's original 2016 release in North America. The character is more popular on a global scale than he's ever been seven decades after his inception. That can't be denied and it's beyond impressive.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

Carson Daly has been a host and a constant presence in my life since the ‘90s. I first became aware of him with his spot as a nighttime host on L.A.’s influential and highly rated alternative rock station KROQ-FM. So, by the time he became a presence on MTV with Total Request Live when the show debuted in 1998, he was already a trusted voice in music and pop culture for me.

Before YouTube and social media, MTV was the place to go if you wanted to be exposed to music you might not have already been aware of yet, and TRL brought heightened awareness to the pop princesses and boy bands of the era. You could catch the hottest music videos of the time while also seeing celebrities drop by to chat with Carson Daly about projects they were promoting.

He always had an ease and comfort with the talent but could also engage with the very passionate viewers as they agreed and disagreed with him. And there’s something comforting about seeing him officially step into the gig as co-host of Saturday Today, all these years later. The Voice host expressed his gratitude to People when reflecting on his latest gig:

I started many years ago at MTV and I feel like I’ve been really lucky. I’ve sort of grown up with an audience. So, if you were 18 and came to TRL, you might be 38 now and have a couple of kids and come to the Plaza. And so, I’ve just been lucky generationally to continue to work in TV, have new opportunities and people have been there with me.

While I never went to TRL in person, and likely won’t make it to the Plaza where they shoot Today, I did tune in often, especially when the likes of Britney Spears or any other popular pop stars were performing, so that I could teach myself the dance steps, to varying degrees of success. I am part of that audience that has grown up with Carson Daly, and I continue to watch him across a variety of projects to this day. And although I do miss the glimpse Total Request Live gave viewers into the lives of the biggest music stars of that era, the most recent attempt at a revival and the decline of MTV in general have made that impossible to recapture.

As someone who has had the successful host on my own TV screen over the decades, I found it particularly touching that when he officially added the Saturday Today co-anchor job in New York City to his already busy schedule that includes shooting The Voice in Los Angeles, he immediately thought of his mother watching the Today Show in their kitchen while he was getting ready for school. He clearly knows how proud his mother would have been to see her son become a part of something that was so important to her own life. Daly explained:

Well, I thought about my mom. My mom, God rest her soul, was the biggest ‘Today Show’ fan of all time. When I was growing up – elementary, junior high and high school – every morning I went in the kitchen, the ‘Today Show’ was on a tiny little TV. And when I got this job, just being here, she was here.

Admitting he teared up over how his mother would feel about his latest hosting gig made me tear up in the process, knowing firsthand how hard it is not to share such a big accomplishment with the one person you know it would mean the most to. He also joked that the other bonus of being gone on Saturday mornings is that it gets him out of making breakfast for his kids, but that they better not DoorDash as a replacement since that’s just too expensive.

There are still rumors that Carson Daly will be leaving The Voice after Season 30 wraps on the 2026 TV schedule, which likely won’t die down anytime soon, especially with Keke Palmer stepping in as host for Season 31’s The Voice: Celebrity. But until we know for sure, the former TRL host can be seen doing his thing on Saturday Today as well as guiding the The Voice singers through the return of the Live Shows as they get closer to announcing a winner in December.
